newsitem.title: ZAIRE: More fighting reported, U.N. searches for refugees.
newsitem.headline: More fighting reported, U.N. searches for refugees.

text.p: Heavy fighting was reported in eastern Zaire on Thursday as rebels, backed by Rwanda, hunted down Hutu gunmen, and the U.N. said it had satellite evidence of large refugee movements in the area.
"Field reports say there is heavy fighting today south of Minova on Lake Kivu, 20 kms (12 miles) south of Sake," U.N. refugee agency UNHCR official Ray Wilkinson told reporters.
"This appears to confirm the reports we've had for the past four days of a large movement of refugees and Interahamwe from south Kivu towards Sake and the north," he said.
The Interahame -- extremist Rwandan Hutu militias -- and troops of the former Rwandan army were ousted by Zairean rebels from refugee camps in eastern Zaire in fighting that started in mid-October.
Some 500,000 Rwandan refugees have since returned home, but the whereabouts of around 700,000 more was unknown after aid workers had to leave the area because of the fighting.

Wilkinson said aid workers would have to contend with "an ongoing diaspora" with people heading in all directions, and that seemed to be confirmed with the findings of satellite photos and overflights, reported by the UNHCR in Geneva.
UNHCR spokeswoman Melita Sunjic told Reuters an estimated 50,000 refugees had been located in an area some 20 km (12 miles) west of the Masisi region, which is west of Goma.
Another estimated 100,000 refugees had been spotted in an area north of Sake village near Masisi town.
And further south, the UNHCR had located some 200,000 refugees around 75 km (45 miles) north of Bukavu and another 250,000 people 75 km (45 miles) south of Bukavu, she said.
Deeper into Zaire, an estimated 100,000 refugees had been seen in Fizi area some 100 km (60 miles) south of Uvira.

Diplomats cautioned that these figures could not be precise, and other reports at odds with the UNHCR details spoke of a large group of refugees heading further and further west over the past three weeks towards Shabunda, 120 kms (75 miles) west of Bukavu.
Field workers said the large group north of Bukavu was apparently trying to go west around Sake in an attempt to link up with Interahamwe groups in Masisi.
Diplomats said this group, and the group reported to have headed west, probably had no intention of returning to Rwanda.
The refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 when a Tutsi-led army overran the country after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus by the Hutu extremists.
Some 500,000 Hutus returned en masse over the past week to escape a new war in which Zairean rebels broke the hold of the militias and former Rwandan army soldiers over them.
There were also reports on Thursday of renewed heavy fighting in the Masisi region, and UNHCR staff in Goma had not been allowed to leave either to the north or south by the rebels, Wilkinson said.
They were told by the soldiers in command at Goma to expect new refugees from the south in the next few days.
"If these reports are correct, it would seemingly signify another major movement of refugees and a very complicated military situation," Wilkinson said.
The United Nations has authorised an intervention force to go to eastern Zaire to help get food to the refugees and allow those that so wished to return home.

Some countries, including the United States, have scaled down their commitment since the 500,000 refugees returned home, but the renewed fighting, with refugees caught in the middle, may give fresh impetus to the Canadian-led mission.
The participating countries are scheduled to meet in Stuttgart on Friday to review the situation.
Emma Bonino, the European Union's aid Commissioner, accused the world community on Thursday of indifference bordering on racism over the plight of the stranded refugees.

"How many lives have to be in danger, how many people missing to justify a deployment of troops by the civilised world'? Who sets the threshold -- is it 500,000, 200,000, 100,000 or 10,000?" she said at the European Parliament.
"Is it the colour of their skin which makes the difference, which leads us to believe that it is their inevitable lot to be linked to a cycle of...massacres?"

She said a proposed U.N. multinational force was essential to allow humanitarian aid workers to save lives in Zaire. Without that protection, aid workers risked being killed and taken hostage, she said.
